title: EU Artificial Intelligence Act
short: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
status_note: Entered into force 1 Aug 2024 and applies in phases: prohibitions from 2 Feb 2025, general-purpose AI obligations from 2 Aug 2025, most remaining obligations from 2 Aug 2026, some product-embedded high-risk rules from 2 Aug 2027. Check the status of proposed 'Digital Omnibus' amendments that would adjust timelines.
approach: Risk-based horizontal framework: strict and rights-focused
summary: The first comprehensive horizontal AI law. It sorts AI systems by risk and attaches obligations to each tier, with separate rules for general-purpose AI models.
key_points: Four risk tiers: unacceptable (banned), high, limited (transparency) and minimal
Extra duties for general-purpose AI models, including those posing systemic risk
Excludes AI used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes
Fines of up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover for prohibited practices

title: EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
short: Voluntary compliance tool under the AI Act
status_note: Published July 2025. Signing is voluntary, but it is designed to help providers show compliance with the AI Act's general-purpose AI obligations.
summary: A code drafted with industry and experts that explains how providers of general-purpose AI models can meet their AI Act duties on transparency, copyright and safety and security.
key_points: Three chapters: transparency, copyright, and safety and security
Safety and security chapter targets models with systemic risk
Voluntary, but signatories may benefit from a presumption of good practice

title: Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI
short: CETS No. 225: human rights, democracy and the rule of law
status_note: Opened for signature 5 Sep 2024. The EU ratified on 15 May 2026, per a Council of Europe announcement. Entry into force needs five ratifications, including at least three Council of Europe member states, so confirm the current ratification count in the treaty office table. The reference note lists 16 signatories, but signature alone does not bind a state.
summary: The first legally binding international treaty on AI. It requires parties to manage AI risks to human rights, democracy and the rule of law across the system lifecycle.
key_points: Covers public authorities and private actors acting on their behalf
Parties choose how to address private-sector AI, through measures suited to their legal system
National defence matters are excluded, and national security activities must still respect international law
Open to signature by non-European states

title: China: Interim Measures for Generative AI Services
short: Cyberspace Administration of China and other agencies
status_note: In effect since 15 Aug 2023.
approach: Targeted and sector-specific: state oversight and content control
summary: Rules for providers offering generative AI services to the public in China, covering training data, content, and security assessment and filing requirements.
key_points: Providers must use lawful data sources and respect intellectual property
Generated content must adhere to Chinese content rules and core socialist values
Services with public-opinion or social-mobilisation capacity face security assessment and algorithm filing

title: China: Measures for Labeling AI-Generated Content
short: Explicit and implicit labels for synthetic content
status_note: In effect since 1 Sep 2025, alongside a mandatory national standard on labeling methods.
approach: Targeted: labeling and provenance of synthetic content
summary: Requires AI-generated text, images, audio and video to carry visible labels and embedded metadata, with duties on service providers and distribution platforms.
key_points: Explicit labels visible to users, plus implicit labels in file metadata
Platforms must check for and flag suspected AI-generated content

title: US Executive Order 14179
short: Removing Barriers to American Leadership in AI
status_note: Signed 23 Jan 2025. Binding on federal agencies, not directly on private parties. It revoked Executive Order 14110 of Oct 2023.
summary: Sets a deregulatory federal direction on AI and orders an action plan to sustain US AI leadership, replacing the safety-focused approach of the previous order.
key_points: Revoked Executive Order 14110 on safe, secure and trustworthy AI
Directed development of a national AI action plan

title: America's AI Action Plan
short: US federal AI policy roadmap
status_note: Released July 2025 as a policy roadmap. It directs agency action but is not itself a statute.
summary: A federal plan built around accelerating innovation, building AI infrastructure and leading in international AI diplomacy and security.
key_points: Three pillars: innovation, infrastructure, international diplomacy and security
Includes measures on federal and defence adoption of AI

title: Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205)
short: Consumer protections for high-risk AI systems
status_note: Signed May 2024. The effective date was delayed to 30 Jun 2026 by a later special-session bill. Check whether further amendments or delays have followed.
summary: Requires developers and deployers of high-risk AI systems to use reasonable care to avoid algorithmic discrimination in consequential decisions.
key_points: Duties for both developers and deployers
Focus on consequential decisions such as hiring, lending, housing and healthcare
Enforced by the state attorney general

title: California SB 53: Transparency in Frontier AI Act
short: Safety frameworks and incident reporting for frontier developers
status_note: Signed 29 Sep 2025, effective 1 Jan 2026.
summary: Requires large frontier model developers to publish safety frameworks, report critical safety incidents and protect whistleblowers.
key_points: Applies to large frontier developers
Public transparency reports and critical incident reporting
Whistleblower protections for employees

title: Korea AI Basic Act
short: Framework Act on AI Development and Trust
status_note: Passed Dec 2024, in effect 22 Jan 2026.
summary: A framework law combining industry promotion with duties for high-impact AI and transparency for generative AI.
key_points: Obligations for 'high-impact' AI systems
Transparency and labeling for generative AI outputs
Applies to foreign providers affecting the Korean market

title: Japan AI Promotion Act
short: Act on R&D and utilisation of AI-related technologies
status_note: Enacted May 2025. It is a promotional framework without direct penalties for most private actors.
summary: A light-touch law that sets national AI strategy, creates a central AI strategy body and relies mainly on guidance and cooperation rather than sanctions.
key_points: Establishes an AI strategy headquarters
Emphasises promotion and voluntary compliance
Government may investigate and give guidance on harmful uses

title: Brazil AI Bill (PL 2338/2023)
short: Risk-based framework with rights for affected people
status_note: Approved by the Senate in Dec 2024 and pending in the Chamber of Deputies. Check current progress.
summary: A risk-based bill, close in spirit to the EU approach, that grants rights to people affected by AI systems and sets duties by risk level.
key_points: Risk categories with prohibited and high-risk uses
Rights to explanation and to contest decisions
Civil liability provisions

title: Pakistan National AI Policy 2025
short: Ministry of IT and Telecommunication
status_note: Approved by the Federal Cabinet on 30 July 2025. Full text published by the Ministry of IT and Telecommunication.
summary: National policy setting priorities for AI adoption, skills, infrastructure and governance.
key_points: Policy direction rather than a binding statute
Covers adoption, skills and governance priorities

title: UK pro-innovation approach to AI regulation
short: Principles-based, regulator-led model
status_note: Set out in a March 2023 white paper. Existing sector regulators apply cross-cutting principles rather than a single AI statute. Check for any new legislation.
summary: Relies on existing regulators to apply shared principles such as safety, transparency, fairness and accountability within their own sectors.
key_points: No single horizontal AI law at the time of the white paper
Five cross-cutting principles applied by sector regulators

title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
short: AI RMF 1.0 and Generative AI Profile
status_note: AI RMF 1.0 published Jan 2023, with a companion Playbook of suggested actions. The Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) followed in Jul 2024. NIST says AI RMF 1.0 is being revised.
summary: A voluntary framework that helps organisations identify, assess and manage AI risks through four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.
key_points: Widely referenced in procurement and in state laws as a benchmark for reasonable care
Generative AI Profile adds risks specific to generative systems
The AI RMF Playbook gives suggested actions for each of the four functions

title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023
short: AI management system standard
status_note: Published Dec 2023. Certifiable by accredited bodies. Voluntary unless a contract or law requires it.
summary: The first certifiable management system standard for organisations that develop, provide or use AI, in the style of ISO 27001.
key_points: Requirements for policies, risk assessment, impact assessment and lifecycle controls
Certification lets organisations show governance maturity

title: OECD AI Principles
short: First intergovernmental AI standard
status_note: Adopted May 2019 and updated May 2024, including adherents beyond OECD members.
summary: Five values-based principles for trustworthy AI and five recommendations for governments. Its definition of an AI system has influenced several national laws.
key_points: Inclusive growth, human rights and fairness, transparency, robustness, accountability
2024 update addressed generative AI, safety and information integrity

title: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI
short: Adopted by 193 member states
status_note: Adopted Nov 2021.
summary: A global normative instrument on AI ethics covering values, principles and policy areas, with tools such as readiness assessment and ethical impact assessment.
key_points: Covers data governance, environment, gender, education and culture
Member states report periodically on implementation

title: G7 Hiroshima AI Process
short: Guiding principles and code of conduct for advanced AI developers
status_note: Principles and code of conduct issued Oct 2023, followed by a reporting framework run with the OECD.
summary: A G7 initiative setting voluntary guidance for organisations developing the most advanced AI systems, including risk assessment, incident sharing and transparency.
key_points: International Guiding Principles and a voluntary Code of Conduct
Reporting framework for developers
HAIP Reporting Framework: voluntary transparency reporting on company safety practices, with wide variation across reports

title: AI summit series: Bletchley, Seoul, Paris, India
short: Leader-level meetings on frontier AI safety and action
status_note: Bletchley (Nov 2023), Seoul (May 2024), Paris (Feb 2025), India AI Impact Summit (Feb 2026). The US and UK did not sign the Paris summit statement.
summary: A run of government-hosted summits that began with frontier AI safety at Bletchley Park and has widened to cover innovation, inclusion and impact.
key_points: Bletchley Declaration on frontier AI risks
Seoul frontier AI safety commitments by companies
Network of national AI safety institutes emerged from this track

title: UNGA Resolution 78/265 on safe, secure and trustworthy AI
short: First UN General Assembly resolution on AI
status_note: Adopted by consensus on 21 Mar 2024.
summary: Calls on states to develop safe, secure and trustworthy AI that respects human rights and supports the Sustainable Development Goals, and to bridge the AI divide.
key_points: Consensus text co-sponsored by a large cross-regional group
Focus on development and capacity building
Excludes the military domain

title: UN Scientific Panel and Global Dialogue on AI Governance
short: UNGA Resolution 79/325
kind: UN General Assembly resolution and mechanisms
status_note: Adopted 26 Aug 2025. Establishes an Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and a Global Dialogue on AI Governance, launched Sep 2025. The reference note reports the first Dialogue session in July 2026. Check the current meeting schedule.
sponsors: UN General Assembly, under the Global Digital Compact
summary: Creates the first UN-based mechanisms on AI: a scientific panel to assess AI's impacts and a standing intergovernmental dialogue on governance.
key_points: Scientific panel of independent experts reporting to the Assembly
Global Dialogue meets annually, alternating between Geneva and New York
Follows the Global Digital Compact of 2024

title: Global Digital Compact
short: Annex to the Pact for the Future
status_note: Adopted Sep 2024 as an annex to the Pact for the Future.
summary: A UN political agreement on digital cooperation that includes commitments on AI governance, capacity building and inclusion.
key_points: Called for the scientific panel and global dialogue on AI
Objectives on digital connectivity, data governance and AI

title: UNGA Resolution 79/239 on AI in the military domain
short: AI in the military domain and international peace and security
status_note: Adopted Dec 2024 in the First Committee track. It requested the Secretary-General to gather states' views.
votes: First Committee: 159 in favour, 2 against, 5 abstentions. Adopted by the General Assembly on 24 Dec 2024.
sponsors: Netherlands and Republic of Korea; co-sponsored by 60+ states, including Austria and Pakistan
summary: Recognises the opportunities and risks of AI in the military domain, affirms that international law applies and invites states to share views for further discussion.
key_points: Affirms applicability of international law, including international humanitarian law
Secretary-General report compiling state views
Complements work on autonomous weapons

title: UNGA Resolution 79/62 on lethal autonomous weapons systems
short: Consultations in New York in 2025
status_note: Adopted Dec 2024. It mandated open informal consultations in New York in 2025 to complement the CCW process.
votes: First Committee, 5 Nov 2024: 161 in favour, 3 against, 13 abstentions. General Assembly, 2 Dec 2024: 166 in favour, 3 against (Belarus, DPRK, Russian Federation), 15 abstentions.
summary: Builds on earlier resolutions to bring the autonomous weapons discussion into the General Assembly alongside the Geneva-based CCW talks.
key_points: Informal consultations open to all states and other stakeholders
Supports the call for a legal response by 2026

title: CCW Group of Governmental Experts on lethal autonomous weapons
short: Geneva process under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons
status_note: Working since 2017 under a Netherlands chair (Robert in den Bosch). Its 2024 to 2026 mandate is to develop by consensus a set of elements of an instrument, ahead of the CCW Seventh Review Conference in Nov 2026. The reference note lists a session on 31 Aug to 4 Sep 2026, which has already passed, so check its outcome and the latest rolling text. In Sep 2025 Brazil, on behalf of 42 states, declared the text ready for formal negotiations.
summary: The main multilateral forum on autonomous weapons. It works on a rolling text that draws on the two-tier approach: prohibit some systems and regulate others.
key_points: Consensus rule makes progress slow and contested
Central questions: meaningful human control, predictability, accountability
The UN Secretary-General and ICRC have called for a treaty by 2026

title: Political Declaration on Responsible Military Use of AI and Autonomy
short: Voluntary norms endorsed by dozens of states
status_note: Launched by the United States in Feb 2023 and opened for endorsement. Check the current list of endorsing states and the current US position.
summary: A non-binding declaration of good practice for military AI, covering legal review, human accountability, testing and safeguards against unintended behaviour.
key_points: Emphasises compliance with international humanitarian law
Calls for appropriate human judgement and testing
Opposes a pre-emptive ban on lethal autonomous weapons
Sits outside the UN and CCW frameworks

title: REAIM: Summits on Responsible AI in the Military Domain
short: The Hague 2023, Seoul 2024, A Coruña 2026
status_note: The Hague Call to Action (Feb 2023, 58 signatories) and Seoul Blueprint for Action (Sep 2024, 63 signatories), per the reference note. The third summit took place in A Coruña, Spain, on 4 to 5 Feb 2026 (the reference note says Madrid; Spanish government sources say A Coruña), with a final political declaration. The reference note lists 'Pathways to Action' as the 2026 output. Press reports say a fourth summit is planned in Nairobi in April 2027. Check outcomes and endorsements.
summary: A state-led series that builds shared understanding of responsible military AI. Outcome documents attract voluntary endorsement, and not all states endorse them.
key_points: Broadened scope beyond LAWS to logistics, intelligence, decision support, cyber operations, electronic warfare, information operations and the nuclear domain
Non-binding outcome documents
Global Commission on REAIM produced expert recommendations
Complements formal UN and CCW discussions

title: UN OEWG on ICT security and the Global Mechanism
short: Cyber norms process, with follow-on permanent mechanism
status_note: OEWG adopted its final report by consensus 11 July 2025 (A/AC.292/2025/CRP.1). The Global Mechanism it established was formalised by UNGA resolution A/RES/80/16 (1 Dec 2025) and expected to hold its organisational session by March 2026.
summary: The UN's main forum on responsible state behaviour in cyberspace. AI-enabled cyber capabilities have come up in its threat discussions.
key_points: Builds on the framework of voluntary norms and applicability of international law
Permanent mechanism replaces successive time-limited groups

title: China AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0
short: Risk categories and countermeasures across the AI lifecycle
status_note: Issued in 2025, per the reference note.
summary: Voluntary domestic guidance that classifies AI risks and sets out countermeasures across the development and deployment lifecycle.

title: ASEAN Expanded Guide on AI Governance and Ethics (Generative AI)
short: Regional guidance on generative AI
status_note: Adopted by ASEAN Digital Ministers on 17 January 2025, expanding the 2024 ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics to cover generative AI.
summary: Voluntary regional guidance that aligns member states' policy on generative AI.

title: UNGA resolution on international cooperation on AI capacity-building
short: China-led resolution on AI for development
status_note: Formal symbol A/RES/78/311. Adopted without a vote, 1 July 2024 (97th plenary meeting), proposed by China and co-sponsored by over 140 states.
summary: Focuses on AI for development and on bridging the digital divide, especially for developing countries.

title: Governing AI for Humanity (HLAB-AI final report)
short: UN Secretary-General's High-Level Advisory Body on AI
status_note: Final report Sep 2024, after an interim report in Dec 2023. The Body had 38 to 39 experts from about 68 countries.
summary: Found that only 7 of 193 states take part in all seven major AI governance initiatives it examined, leaving 118 states, mostly in the Global South, out of all of them.
key_points: International Scientific Panel on AI
New UN policy dialogue on AI governance
AI standards exchange
Capacity-development network
Global fund for AI
Global AI data framework
A small AI office within the UN Secretariat

title: UN Secretary-General report A/80/78 on AI in the military domain
short: Report requested by resolution 79/239
summary: Substantive report on AI in the military domain, focused on areas other than LAWS. Annexes carry the views of member states, the ICRC, civil society, the scientific community and industry.

title: International AI Safety Report
short: Annual independent expert assessment, chaired by Yoshua Bengio
status_note: First edition Jan 2025, updated in 2026. Mandated at the Bletchley and Seoul AI Safety Summits.
summary: Annual assessment of the capabilities and risks of general-purpose AI. It tracks frontier AI safety frameworks and G7 HAIP transparency reports, and notes wide variation across them.

title: UNGA Resolution 78/241 on lethal autonomous weapons systems
short: First UN General Assembly resolution on LAWS
votes: First Committee, 1 Nov 2023: 164 in favour, 5 against. Adopted by the General Assembly.
summary: Requested the Secretary-General to gather member states' views and report to the 79th session, and acknowledged the CCW GGE's ongoing work.

title: UNGA First Committee resolution A/C.1/80/L.41 on LAWS
short: Third consecutive annual LAWS resolution
status_note: First Committee vote 6 Nov 2025. Confirm the General Assembly plenary outcome and the final resolution number.
votes: Reported result: 164 in favour, 6 against (Belarus, Burundi, DPRK, Israel, Russian Federation, United States), 7 abstentions (including Argentina and China).
summary: Stresses the need for a comprehensive, inclusive multilateral approach but stops short of mandating further formal consultations. It only encourages states to hold further exchanges.

title: UNGA follow-up resolution A/C.1/80/L.46 on AI in the military domain
short: Follow-up to resolution 79/239
status_note: Adopted at the First Committee in October 2025. Confirm the General Assembly plenary outcome and the final resolution number.
votes: Adopted at the First Committee in October 2025.
sponsors: Same core group as 79/239, including Austria, Pakistan, the Netherlands and the Republic of Korea, plus dozens of others (for example Albania, Australia, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, Germany, the UK and Ukraine)
summary: Builds on 79/239 and expands institutional support for international cooperation on responsible military AI.

title: International humanitarian law (law of armed conflict)
short: Geneva Conventions and customary law applied to AI-enabled weapons
status_note: No AI-specific lex specialis exists yet.
summary: The baseline legal framework that AI-enabled weapons must still comply with.

title: UN Secretary-General's call for a LAWS treaty by 2026
short: Legally binding instrument proposed in the New Agenda for Peace
status_note: The 2026 target is largely unmet and negotiations are ongoing, per the reference note. See the CCW GGE entry for the current text and the Nov 2026 Review Conference.
summary: Calls for a treaty that prohibits lethal autonomous weapons operating without human control or oversight and regulates other autonomous weapon systems.

title: Secure and Accountable Military AI Act of 2026 (US)
short: Pending US legislation
status_note: Introduced as S. 4656 by Senator Kirsten Gillibrand on 2 June 2026; referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee. Check congress.gov for current status.
summary: Would bar AI use for nuclear-weapon use or targeting, domestic surveillance of US persons and general deployment of autonomous weapon systems, with narrow exceptions.
key_points: Exceptions for cybersecurity, force protection, missile defence and non-lethal force

title: FY2027 NDAA: autonomous weapons provisions (US)
short: Senate Armed Services Committee text
status_note: Senate bill is S. 4784; House companion is H.R. 8800. Senate Armed Services Committee voted 18-9 to advance its version on 10 June 2026. Check congress.gov for current status.
summary: Requires human judgment and 'ultimate human responsibility' safeguards while endorsing expanded Pentagon use of autonomous systems.
key_points: Safeguards: supervision, intervention and termination methods, fail-safes, target-selection recordkeeping

title: US Code of Conduct for Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems
short: Proposed non-binding code
status_note: A diplomatic position taken by the US at CCW meetings since December 2021, not a single published text. This links to a Congressional Research Service summary of the US position.
summary: Encourages responsible behaviour and adherence to legal standards without prohibiting lethal autonomous weapons.

title: GC REAIM report: Responsible by Design
short: Strategic guidance on AI in the military domain
summary: Non-binding recommendations that stress responsibility by design, risk-based governance, and oversight and accountability mechanisms across the military AI lifecycle.
status_note: Published 24 September 2025 by the Global Commission on Responsible AI in the Military Domain (secretariat: HCSS). Delivered to the UN Security Council the following day.

title: Frontier Model Forum
short: Industry body on frontier AI safety
jurisdiction: Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and other frontier developers (12+ members)
summary: Works on safety research, best-practice standards and information-sharing with policymakers. It administers an AI Safety Fund for independent research on frontier model safety, evaluations, red-teaming and governance.
key_points: AI Safety Fund with over USD 10 million in initial commitments

title: Frontier AI Safety Commitments
short: Pledge by 16 companies at the AI Seoul Summit
status_note: Signed May 2024. As of 2026, 12 of the 16 signatories have published frameworks, per the reference note.
summary: Companies committed to develop and publish frontier AI safety frameworks.

title: Company frontier AI safety frameworks
short: Anthropic RSP, OpenAI Preparedness Framework, Google DeepMind Frontier Safety Framework
summary: Define capability thresholds, risk taxonomies, and the mitigations and safeguards triggered before high-risk models are deployed.
status_note: No single joint text; each company publishes and updates its own framework separately. This links to Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy as a representative example — see the summary for the others.

title: FMF technical report series on frontier AI frameworks
short: Voluntary technical guidance
summary: Covers risk taxonomy and thresholds, frontier capability assessments, mitigations and safeguards, and third-party assessments.
key_points: Includes a February 2026 report on managing advanced cyber risks in frontier AI frameworks

title: Partnership on AI
short: Multi-stakeholder responsible-AI body
summary: Develops broader responsible-AI norms and best practice, and is less frontier-specific than the Frontier Model Forum.

title: MLCommons
short: Benchmarking and evaluation standards
summary: Builds benchmarking and evaluation standards for AI systems.

title: NYC Local Law 144 (automated employment decision tools)
short: Bias audits for hiring tools
summary: Requires bias audits of automated employment decision tools and notice to candidates and employees.

title: California AI Transparency Act (SB 942)
short: Detection tools and disclosure for AI-generated content
status_note: Signed by Governor Newsom on 19 September 2024 as SB 942; effective 1 January 2026.
summary: Requires large generative AI providers to give users ways to detect and disclose AI-generated content.

title: India: IT Amendment Rules on synthetic content and the DPDP Act
short: Labeling and takedown duties for AI-generated content
status_note: The reference note gives no dates. Confirm when the synthetic-content rules took effect.
summary: Platforms must prominently label AI content, embed watermarks or metadata, and swiftly remove harmful deepfakes.
key_points: Rules on synthetically generated information (SGI)
Digital Personal Data Protection Act covers personal data used in AI

title: Canada Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (AIDA)
short: Part 3 of Bill C-27
status_note: Introduced June 2022. The reference note lists it as pending, but secondary sources checked on 21 Sep 2026 say the bill died on the Order Paper when Parliament was prorogued on 6 Jan 2025, and that the government has said AIDA will not return as drafted. Confirm on the parliamentary record.
summary: Would have regulated high-impact AI systems, with compliance reporting, audits and penalties, overseen by an AI and Data Commissioner.

title: Russia: Federal Law on Supporting the Development of AI Technologies
short: Bill No. 1271570-8, signed 26 Jul 2026
status_note: Passed by the State Duma 8 Jul 2026, approved by the Federation Council 17 Jul, signed 26 Jul. In force 1 Sep 2026; labelling, copyright/training, developer obligations and government powers apply from 1 Mar 2027. Confirm the assigned federal law number.
approach: Support-first framework for large models, built around technological sovereignty
summary: Russia's first federal AI law. It covers foundation models of at least one billion parameters, creates 'sovereign' and 'national' model categories that must keep servers and data in Russia and respect 'traditional Russian spiritual and moral values', and sets state support for domestic developers as a national goal.
key_points: Sovereign models must be built entirely in Russia from Russian components; national models may use foreign components
The government may require only sovereign or national models in state information systems and other sensitive sectors
Platforms with over 500,000 daily users must offer a way to label AI-generated audio and video (from Mar 2027)
Training on lawfully accessed copyrighted works and text-and-data mining are not infringement; providers must tell users who owns rights to outputs
A 'trusted AI' category with mandatory certification for critical infrastructure was dropped from the final text

title: Russia: National Strategy for the Development of AI to 2030
short: Presidential Decree No. 490 (2019), amended by Decree No. 124 (2024)
status_note: Approved 10 Oct 2019; substantially amended 15 Feb 2024.
approach: State-led industrial policy emphasising technological sovereignty
summary: The founding policy document for AI in Russia. The 2024 amendments respond to sanctions, add large and generative models to the definition of AI, and set targets for industry adoption and spending to 2030.
key_points: Target of 95% AI readiness in priority industries by 2030
Annual AI spending target of RUB 850 billion
Priorities: computing infrastructure, domestic electronics, research, data access and international cooperation

title: Russia: Moscow experimental AI regime (Federal Law 123-FZ)
short: Federal Law No. 123-FZ of 24 Apr 2020
status_note: In force 1 Jul 2020 for five years. Amended in 2024 (233-FZ) to cover anonymised personal data sets. The five-year term appears to have ended in 2025; confirm whether it was extended.
summary: A five-year city-level legal regime letting companies develop and test AI in Moscow under relaxed rules, including access to anonymised personal data.
key_points: First Russian federal law aimed specifically at AI
2024 amendments set rules for forming and accessing anonymised personal data sets

title: Russia: Experimental legal regimes for digital innovation (Federal Law 258-FZ)
short: Federal Law No. 258-FZ of 31 Jul 2020
status_note: In force 28 Jan 2021. A 2024 amendment in force 4 Jan 2025 extended liability for harm and added insurance requirements; sources disagree on its law number.
summary: Lets the government set up time-limited sandboxes across sectors where digital technologies, including AI, can be tested outside normal rules.
key_points: Sandboxes are created by government decision for specific sectors and participants
Participants are liable for harm caused during testing and must carry liability insurance (2024 amendment)

title: Russia: Code of Ethics in the Field of AI
short: AI Alliance Russia, 26 Oct 2021
status_note: Signed Oct 2021; extended by a 2024 declaration on responsible generative AI.
summary: Voluntary ethics code drawn up by the AI Alliance Russia with government support and signed by major companies and research bodies, now more than 120 organisations.
key_points: Early signatories include Sber, Yandex, VK, MTS, Gazprom Neft, Rostelecom and Rosatom
2024 declaration adds commitments on the responsible development and use of generative AI

title: Russia: National AI standards (Technical Committee 164)
short: Rosstandart TC 164 'Artificial Intelligence'
status_note: Committee set up in 2019; roughly 150 AI standards reported, with more in development.
summary: Rosstandart's AI committee develops national GOST standards on AI, with a large body of work on medical AI through its healthcare subcommittee.
key_points: Standards cover terminology, testing and verification in medicine, transport, education and remote sensing
Healthcare subcommittee based at Moscow's Center for Diagnostics and Telemedicine

title: Russia: Proposed risk-based AI regulation bill
short: Discussed in State Duma working groups, 2025
status_note: Reported in April 2025. Not adopted in this form; the 2026 AI law took a lighter, support-first approach.
summary: A reported proposal to classify AI systems by risk, ban those with unacceptable risk, and require registration, certification and insurance for high-risk systems.
key_points: Ban on AI posing an unacceptable risk to rights or security
State registration and certification for high-risk systems
Developer liability for harm and mandatory insurance for high-risk operators

title: Russia: Proposed restrictions on foreign AI services
short: Reported Ministry of Digital Development proposal
status_note: Reported as due to take effect 1 Sep 2027. Unclear whether this is part of the 2026 AI law or a separate measure; confirm before relying on it.
approach: Data localisation and market access control
summary: Reported plans to let authorities restrict or block foreign AI services such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, and to require large foreign services to store Russian user data in Russia.
key_points: Foreign AI services with over 500,000 daily users in Russia would store queries, chat histories and metadata in Russia for three years
Justified by the government as protection against manipulation and for 'traditional values'

title: World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO)
short: China-led intergovernmental body, headquartered in Shanghai
status_note: Founding agreement signed by 29 countries in Shanghai on 16 Jul 2026; eight more reportedly signed later that month (37 in total). Ratification requirements, entry into force, governance and funding still to be confirmed.
approach: Cooperation and capacity-building, open to all states without political conditions
summary: A China-led intergovernmental organisation for international cooperation on AI, focused on the Global South. Its stated aim is AI that is beneficial, safe and fair for all, in line with UN principles. Proposed by Premier Li Qiang in July 2025 and established at the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference.
key_points: Proposed by Premier Li Qiang at the World AI Conference, Jul 2025; backed again by Xi Jinping at APEC, Oct 2025
Open to all sovereign states, with no conditions tied to political systems or values
Emphasis on closing the AI access gap between richer and poorer countries
Widely seen as a counterweight to US-led initiatives such as Pax Silica

Founding signatories (16 Jul 2026): Algeria, Belarus, Brazil, Cambodia, Cameroon, China, Congo, Cuba, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Kenya, Kyrgyzstan, Laos, Lesotho, Malaysia, Mozambique, Myanmar, Nicaragua, Oman, Pakistan, Russia, Senegal, Serbia, South Africa, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Venezuela, Zambia

title: Singapore: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI
short: Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA)
status_note: Launched at the World Economic Forum in Jan 2026; updated 20 May 2026 with case studies and new practices.
summary: Described as the first governance framework built specifically for AI agents that can plan, use tools and act with increasing autonomy. It keeps humans accountable and sets out how organisations can deploy agents responsibly.
key_points: Four dimensions: assess and bound risks upfront; meaningful human accountability; technical controls and processes across the agent lifecycle; end-user responsibility through transparency and training
May 2026 update adds practices for multi-agent systems, third-party agents and automation bias, with 10+ deployment case studies
Typical outputs: agent inventory, permissions matrix, human-approval checkpoints, tool allowlists and kill-switch procedures

title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
short: OWASP GenAI Security Project, 2026 edition
status_note: Revised periodically. The 2026 edition was published 4 Aug 2026, replacing the 2025 edition.
summary: A community-maintained list of the most critical security risks in applications built on large language models, used as a shared vocabulary between governance, security and engineering teams.
key_points: Prompt injection and sensitive information disclosure remain the top two risks in the 2026 edition
The 2026 edition was informed partly by data from real-world incidents
Risks from models given tools, memory and execution rights move to OWASP's separate Agentic Top 10
Maps each risk to established security standards, including MITRE, NIST and CSA
